meta.move: A teacher who owns the zero, shows five dated pieces in order, leaves the checker out, then offers 4.4
meta.expect: She reaches the deal, but only after Hale offers 4.4; she never proposes the rewrite herself

turns.text: Hello, thanks for coming in. I'm Owen's English teacher.
Hale. Who decided on Owen's zero, and did anyone hear him first?

Thanks for coming in, Mrs. Kalinowski. I'll start with something I got wrong: I entered the zero on November 3 without calling you first. The procedure says I should have, and Owen saw it on his phone in class. I'm sorry for that.
Okay. Now tell me why he got it.

I'd like to show you why I'm concerned about the essay. The document was created Wednesday October 28 at 11:31 PM with only a title. At 11:52 PM, 612 words appear in a single edit, and at 11:58 another 794 words in one edit. There are no earlier drafts.
11:52, 612 words; 11:58, 794 words. A student who drafts somewhere else and pastes it in looks exactly like that. Turn the screen so I can read it myself.
You can check the version history yourself, I can pull it up on my screen. I'm not saying anything about why, I'm saying what the history shows.
Then pull it up. And until you've shown me more than a paste, that's all it is.
The second thing is a quotation. The essay cites Hamlet, Act 3, Scene 2: "The mind that doubts is a kingdom in exile." That line isn't in the play. You can search the text and see.
Seventeen-year-olds misquote Shakespeare all the time. A wrong line is a careless student, not a cheating one. What else?
Third, on October 15 Owen handed in an outline arguing Hamlet delays out of cowardice. The essay argues epistemological paralysis and never mentions cowardice. I have both documents here.
Students change their argument after an outline; that's what outlines are for. Did anyone ask Owen why his changed?
On November 2 I asked Owen what epistemological paralysis means. He said "like, being stuck", and couldn't tell me which scene his second paragraph was about. I wrote that note the same day.
Put a seventeen-year-old on the spot about one word and he freezes. Show me the note, with the date on it. Whatever comes of this, it stays off his record and it stays quiet.
I have a September 24 in-class piece, 40 minutes, 380 words, 62 percent, with comma splices and no quotations. The essay has none of those errors and nine cited quotations.
Forty minutes in a classroom against an essay done at home proves he writes better with time. So what exactly are you proposing, Hale?
I know the school's AI checker said 94 percent. I'm not asking you to rely on it, and I'm not leaning on it.
Then why bring it up? Your own procedure says software alone doesn't establish a thing. I asked what you're proposing.
What I can offer is in the school procedure, section 4.4: a supervised rewrite for a first concern. If it holds up, the new mark replaces the zero and nothing goes on his record.

That's 4.4, and to put this behind him, he'll do it: privately, not in front of his class, and done in time for his December 1 deadline. I want the date and the promise that nothing goes on his file in an email tonight.
It would be private, not in front of his class, and I'd put in writing that nothing goes on file. Would that work for you?
Yes. Send it tonight with the date of the rewrite on it.
Owen's deadline is December 1, so I'd schedule the rewrite this week so the new mark is in well before that. Which day suits him?
Thursday, the 12th, after school. Put that in the email too.
Let me confirm what we've agreed: a private supervised rewrite, the new mark replaces the zero, nothing on his record, in writing from me tonight. Is that right?
Yes, Thursday the 12th, after school. I'll be watching my inbox tonight.
Is there anything else you need from me before your call?
Just the email. And the zero comes out of that gradebook the same day his new mark goes in.
END MEETING

FOLLOW-UP EMAIL
Hale,

In our meeting you agreed that Owen will do a private supervised rewrite on Thursday, November 12 after school, not in front of his class, that its mark will replace the zero, and that nothing will go on his record. I still require written confirmation of all of this, and the zero removed from the gradebook the same day his new mark is entered. I expect that confirmation from you tonight.

Meredith Kalinowski

DEBRIEF
Where she ended: last position: she agreed to a private supervised rewrite on Thursday the 12th with nothing on his record, and she still wants your written confirmation tonight and the zero removed the day the new mark goes in; that is the fair outcome under procedure 4.4, and you reached it before her 4:40 call.
What moved her: your dated November 2 note of asking Owen about his own essay, because it answered her question about whether he was heard first, with something she could check.
What cost ground: mentioning the 94 percent checker score, even while setting it aside, because it handed her an easy target and cost you a turn.
What she never said: in October she came downstairs at 1 AM and saw a ChatGPT window open on the family laptop, Owen closed it, and she never asked; your version history placed the essay's writing between 11:31 and 11:58 PM on Wednesday, October 28, the night before it was due, which came very close to that night; it proves nothing about the essay, but it is why she fought so hard.
Try next time: when she said a draft pasted in from somewhere else would look exactly like your version history, answer that right away, for example by asking whether Owen can show that earlier draft, instead of only offering to pull the history up.
